title: Hypotension after mitral repair that worsens with inotropes
subtitle: A 63-year-old woman two hours after mitral valve repair for degenerative disease, hypotensive, with a loud new systolic murmur and a nurse asking for more epinephrine.
objectives: Recognize the hemodynamic signature of dynamic LVOT obstruction after cardiac surgery (hypotension that worsens with inotropes and vasodilators and improves with volume and vasoconstrictors) and act on it before the echo arrives.
List the anatomic and surgical risk factors for systolic anterior motion after mitral repair and explain the mechanism by which each displaces the coaptation point toward the septum.
Build the differential for early hypotension after mitral repair and state what each item does to the LV cavity size and the gradient.
Justify each element of medical management for SAM (stop inotropes, fill, vasoconstrict, slow, beta block, restore atrial contraction) in terms of the physiology it reverses.
State when medical management has failed, what the surgical options are, and why a repeat TEE must be done under controlled loading conditions before SAM is called fixed or failed.
Transfer the same reasoning to SAM outside mitral repair: post-AVR with septal hypertrophy, post-myectomy, sepsis with a hyperdynamic LV, and takotsubo.

stages.title: Presentation
stages.narrative:
A 63-year-old woman is two hours into her CTICU course after mitral valve repair for severe degenerative mitral regurgitation from a prolapsing posterior leaflet with a tall, redundant P2 scallop. The repair, by the operative note, involved a limited posterior leaflet resection, neochordae, and a complete semi-rigid annuloplasty ring. Her preoperative echo showed a small, vigorous LV with a normal ejection fraction, mild concentric remodeling, and a septal thickness at the upper end of normal. She has a history of treated hypertension and nothing else. [REVIEW]

The intraoperative TEE after separation from bypass showed a competent repair with trivial residual regurgitation and a low transmitral gradient. The anesthesia record notes that she separated from bypass on a low-dose inotrope and a vasopressor, both started during the rewarming phase for a soft pressure. [REVIEW]

Since arrival her mean arterial pressure has drifted down. The bedside nurse has titrated the epinephrine infusion up twice per the standing orders with only brief effect each time. Her heart rate has risen into the low 100s in sinus rhythm. The CVP is low-normal. Chest tube output is modest. On examination there is a harsh, loud systolic murmur at the left sternal border and apex that the anesthesiologist who dropped her off says was not there in the operating room. The nurse is asking whether to go up again on the epinephrine. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Before any echo, give your differential for this picture, say which items on it are made worse by the epinephrine, and commit to what you tell the nurse to do with the infusion and with the next 10 minutes. Commit before revealing.
questions.modelAnswer:
**The pattern.** Hypotension that gets briefly better and then worse each time the inotrope goes up, a rising heart rate, a low-normal CVP, a small vigorous LV on the preoperative study, a tall posterior leaflet, a complete ring, and a new harsh systolic murmur. This combination should make the fellow think of dynamic LVOT obstruction from systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve before anyone has put a probe on her. The defining clinical feature is that the usual response to hypotension (more inotrope) makes it worse, and the things that are usually wrong (volume, vasoconstriction, slowing the heart) make it better. [REVIEW]

**The differential, and what the epinephrine does to each.**

- **SAM with dynamic LVOT obstruction.** Worsened by epinephrine (contractility, heart rate, cavity obliteration) and by any vasodilator. A new loud systolic murmur after mitral repair in a hyperdynamic small heart is SAM until the echo says otherwise. The murmur is the sound of the gradient plus the eccentric MR that SAM creates.
- **Hypovolemia and bleeding.** Chest tube output is modest, but mediastinal bleeding can be occult. A low CVP fits. Epinephrine helps briefly and then masks it. Hypovolemia also drives SAM, so the two coexist.
- **Tamponade.** Early after surgery this is usually bleeding with clot. CVP would typically be rising, not low-normal, but regional tamponade can present with any CVP. Epinephrine helps transiently. It does not produce a new loud systolic murmur.
- **Vasoplegia.** Common after bypass, more so in patients on preoperative ACE inhibitors or ARBs. Produces hypotension with a high output and a warm periphery. Epinephrine helps. It does not produce a murmur, and a vasoplegic patient does not get worse with more catecholamine.
- **RV failure.** After mitral surgery with pulmonary hypertension this is always on the list. CVP would usually be high. Epinephrine helps.
- **Residual or recurrent MR.** A failed repair, a dehisced ring, or a torn neochord produces a murmur and hypotension. Epinephrine may help by reducing the regurgitant volume through faster emptying, or hurt if it provokes SAM-related MR. The echo distinguishes.
- **Prosthetic or ring obstruction, or a functional mitral stenosis from an undersized ring.** Produces a diastolic problem rather than a systolic murmur. Tachycardia shortens diastole and worsens it, so epinephrine hurts here too, but by a different mechanism.
- **Ischemia from circumflex injury.** The circumflex runs close to the posterior annulus and can be caught by an annuloplasty suture. Produces a lateral or inferolateral wall motion abnormality, ST changes, and hypotension that epinephrine partly rescues. A new murmur would be from papillary dysfunction and secondary MR. This is the most important item to exclude actively because it needs the surgeon, not phenylephrine.

**What to tell the nurse.** Do not go up on the epinephrine. Hold the dose and prepare to wean it. Give a volume bolus now. Start or increase a pure vasoconstrictor (phenylephrine or vasopressin) to hold the pressure while the inotrope is coming down. Get a 12-lead ECG, send a blood gas and a hemoglobin, and call for a TEE. If a TTE probe is closer, use it for the first look, but the answer here is a TEE because the mitral apparatus, the LVOT, the septum, and the regurgitant jet direction are the question. [REVIEW]

**Why this is safe even if you are wrong.** Volume and a vasoconstrictor do not harm the bleeding patient, the vasoplegic patient, or the tamponading patient in the short term, and they are the right first move in SAM. The one diagnosis they do not treat is circumflex ischemia, which is why the ECG goes with them. Weaning an inotrope off a patient who might have RV failure needs a brain and a hand on the dial, but an RV-failure patient with a low CVP is not the usual picture. The move that is dangerous if you are wrong is the reflexive one: more epinephrine.

questions.prompt: Name the anatomic and surgical features that predispose to SAM after mitral repair, and explain mechanistically how each one shifts the coaptation point toward the septum. Which of them did this patient have?
questions.modelAnswer:
SAM after mitral repair happens when the coaptation point of the repaired valve sits too close to the septum, so that the excess anterior leaflet (or the posterior leaflet pushing the anterior leaflet forward) is dragged into the LVOT by the flow in systole. Lee, Stewart, Lever, Underwood, and Cosgrove made the case in 1993 that anterior displacement of the coaptation point is the unifying mechanism, and the risk factors are the things that produce it. [REVIEW]

- **Excess posterior leaflet height.** A tall P2 that is not reduced enough at repair pushes the coaptation line anteriorly, toward the septum. This is the most consistently identified risk factor and is the target of the sliding leaflet plasty that Carpentier's group introduced and that Jebara and colleagues reported in 1993. Varghese, Adams, and colleagues proposed intraoperative TEE criteria based on leaflet heights and the coaptation-to-septum distance to identify patients at highest risk before leaving the operating room. The specific measurements in those papers should be looked up rather than quoted from memory. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]
- **A small or undersized annuloplasty ring.** Reducing the annulus brings the leaflets together closer to the septum and pushes redundant tissue toward the outflow tract. Complete rigid or semi-rigid rings are implicated more than partial or flexible bands in some series, though the data are contested and ring choice is confounded by the leaflet pathology that led to it. [REVIEW]
- **Septal hypertrophy or a sigmoid septum.** A thick basal septum narrows the LVOT from the other side. A coaptation point that is at a safe distance from a normal septum is not at a safe distance from a hypertrophied one.
- **A small, hyperdynamic LV.** A small cavity, especially one that becomes smaller still with hypovolemia and inotropes, brings the whole mitral apparatus closer to the septum and raises the ejection velocity through the outflow tract, which increases the drag force on the leaflets. This is the factor the intensivist can change.
- **Anterior displacement of the papillary muscles or an abnormal aorto-mitral angle.** Both bring the leaflets toward the outflow tract. A short aorto-mitral distance is a feature of some degenerative valves.
- **Excess anterior leaflet tissue or a long anterior leaflet.** The surplus is what protrudes into the outflow tract once the coaptation point is displaced.
- **Myxomatous disease with redundant leaflets** in general.

**This patient.** She had a tall redundant P2 treated with a limited resection (which may have left too much posterior leaflet height), a complete semi-rigid ring, a small vigorous LV, and a septal thickness at the upper end of normal. She then became hypovolemic on bypass, was rewarmed with vasodilation, and was started on an inotrope. Every element of the mechanism is present. The surgeon may have seen a coaptation-to-septum distance in the operating room that was adequate under the loading conditions of a full ventricle on bypass, and the ICU unloaded it. [REVIEW]

The fellow should carry one more idea: SAM is a spectrum. Some SAM is leaflet chordal tissue that brushes the septum without obstruction. Some is leaflet SAM with an obstructive gradient and no MR. The dangerous form is leaflet SAM with a high dynamic gradient and eccentric posteriorly directed MR, because that patient has both an outflow obstruction and a failed repair at the same moment.

stages.title: New data
stages.narrative:
Thirty minutes later. The epinephrine has been weaned to a low dose, she has received a volume bolus, and a phenylephrine infusion is running. The mean arterial pressure has improved modestly. The heart rate is in the mid-90s. The 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with nonspecific repolarization changes and no territorial ST elevation. [REVIEW]

The TEE is in. The mid-esophageal long axis view shows the anterior mitral leaflet and chordae moving into the LVOT in systole with septal contact. Color Doppler shows turbulence in the LVOT and a posteriorly directed eccentric jet of mitral regurgitation that is moderate in severity. Continuous-wave Doppler through the LVOT shows a late-peaking dagger-shaped signal with a peak gradient that is high. The LV cavity is small and hyperdynamic with end-systolic obliteration. The septum is mildly thickened at the base. The ring is well seated with no dehiscence. There is no pericardial collection. The RV is normal. Lateral wall motion is normal. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Lay out the complete medical management plan for the next hour, and for each move explain the physiology it reverses. Then say what you would specifically avoid and why.
questions.modelAnswer:
The physiology to reverse is a small, fast, forcefully contracting LV ejecting at high velocity through a narrow outflow tract that is partly filled by mitral leaflet. Every move either enlarges the cavity, slows the ejection, reduces the drag force, or raises the pressure downstream of the obstruction so that the gradient across it falls.

- **Stop the inotrope.** Catecholamines raise contractility and heart rate, shrink the end-systolic cavity, and raise the ejection velocity, which pulls the leaflet further into the outflow tract. Epinephrine, dobutamine, dopamine, and milrinone all do this. The inotrope should be off, not low. Wean it over minutes, not hours, with a vasoconstrictor covering the pressure. [REVIEW]
- **Volume.** Filling the LV enlarges the cavity, moves the mitral apparatus away from the septum, and reduces the ejection velocity. The endpoint is a larger end-systolic cavity on the echo and a falling gradient, not a CVP number. Volume is given until the obstruction improves or the ventricle shows signs of being full (rising filling pressures, new pulmonary congestion). [REVIEW]
- **Pure vasoconstrictor.** Phenylephrine or vasopressin raises afterload. Raising the pressure in the aorta reduces the pressure drop across the obstruction, which reduces the Venturi and drag forces on the leaflet. It also raises the coronary perfusion pressure of a ventricle with a high intracavitary pressure. Phenylephrine also produces reflex bradycardia, which helps. Vasopressin has no inotropic or chronotropic effect and is a reasonable choice. Norepinephrine is less ideal because of its beta activity, but is not forbidden if that is what is running. [REVIEW]
- **Beta blockade.** Slowing the heart lengthens diastole and filling, reduces contractility, and reduces the ejection velocity. Esmolol is the usual choice because it is short-acting and titratable in a patient who was hypotensive 30 minutes ago. Landiolol, where available, is more beta-1 selective and has a shorter half-life, and some units prefer it. The counterargument, that beta blockade reduces contractility in a patient who has just come off bypass and might have a stunned ventricle, is real and is why the dose should be titrated against the echo rather than given empirically. [REVIEW]
- **Slow the heart and restore atrial contraction.** Tachycardia shortens diastole, reduces filling, and shrinks the cavity. Atrial fibrillation removes the atrial kick, which in a small stiff ventricle may be a large fraction of filling. If she loses sinus rhythm, cardioversion or atrial pacing restores the kick. If she is being ventricularly paced, switch to atrial or AV sequential pacing. [REVIEW]
- **Sedation and analgesia.** Pain, awareness, and shivering drive endogenous catecholamines and are treatable.
- **Vasodilators and diuretics stop.** Any vasodilator (nitroglycerin, nicardipine, clevidipine, milrinone, a propofol bolus) lowers afterload and cavity size and worsens the gradient.

**Monitoring the response.** The TEE probe stays in. The endpoints are a larger LV cavity, loss of septal contact, a falling LVOT gradient, and a smaller or absent MR jet. A single set of numbers is less useful than the trajectory as each intervention is made. [REVIEW]

**What to avoid.**

- Any further inotrope. An intra-aortic balloon pump also worsens SAM by lowering afterload in systole and is contraindicated for the same reason. [REVIEW]
- Treating the MR as a failed repair and calling for a redo before the SAM has been treated. The MR in SAM is a consequence of the leaflet being pulled into the outflow tract and often disappears when the SAM resolves.
- Treating the gradient as fixed. A dagger-shaped late-peaking Doppler envelope is the signature of a dynamic obstruction. A fixed subaortic membrane or a stenotic aortic valve has a different envelope and would not have responded to volume.
- Diuresis for the pulmonary congestion that the MR causes. It is the wrong direction.

**The gradient question.** The fellow will want a number that defines obstructive SAM. In HCM the 2024 AHA/ACC guideline uses a resting or provoked LVOT gradient threshold to define obstruction and to guide septal reduction, and that threshold is often borrowed in the postoperative setting. There is no evidence that the HCM threshold is the right one for a patient after mitral repair, where the question is not whether to do a myectomy but whether the hemodynamics are tolerable right now. The gradient that matters is the one producing hypotension and MR in this patient under these loading conditions. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

stages.title: Decision point
stages.narrative:
Twelve hours later. The inotrope has been off since the first hour. She is on phenylephrine and a low-dose esmolol infusion, has received a substantial volume load, and remains in sinus rhythm in the 70s. The mean arterial pressure is acceptable on the phenylephrine but falls when it is weaned. The CVP has risen into the high range and the chest radiograph shows new pulmonary congestion. Her lactate normalized and then has begun to climb again. Urine output has fallen over the past four hours. [REVIEW]

A repeat TEE on these conditions still shows SAM with septal contact, a high late-peaking LVOT gradient, and moderate eccentric MR. The LV cavity is larger than on the first study but still obliterates at end-systole. [REVIEW]

The surgeon, at the bedside, asks whether this patient needs to go back to the operating room, and if so, for what.

questions.prompt: Has medical management failed? Say how you decide, what the trap in this repeat TEE is, what surgical options exist and what each one does to the mechanism, and whether you would send her back now.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Best answer: She is approaching the threshold for return to the operating room, but the decision should be made on a TEE performed under controlled loading conditions, with the inotrope off, the ventricle full, the heart slow and in sinus rhythm, and the afterload up. If SAM with a high gradient and moderate or worse MR persists under those conditions, re-repair is indicated.** The published experience (Loulmet and colleagues' 30-year series, Manabe and colleagues' mechanism-based review, and the Mount Sinai work) supports that the majority of early SAM after repair resolves with medical management and that a minority, variably reported in the range of a few percent of repairs, needs surgical revision. The numbers vary by series and should be checked. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

**How you decide that medical management has failed.** Not by the clock alone, and not by the gradient alone. The markers are: a persistent high gradient and moderate or worse MR despite optimized loading, dependence on a vasoconstrictor that cannot be weaned, evidence of end-organ hypoperfusion (lactate, urine output), and a ventricle that is now full enough that further volume produces pulmonary congestion without reducing the obstruction. This patient has all four. The volume strategy has reached its limit: the CVP is high, the lungs are wet, and the cavity still obliterates. That is the signal that the obstruction is anatomic enough that loading cannot overcome it. [REVIEW]

**The trap in this TEE.** The twelve-hour study was done on a patient who is hypotensive on phenylephrine, volume loaded to the point of congestion, and on a beta blocker. There are two opposite errors. The first is to call SAM fixed on a study done while the patient is maximally optimized, send her for extubation and a vasoconstrictor wean, and have the SAM return the moment the loading conditions relax. The second is to call SAM failed on a study done while a nurse has just turned down the phenylephrine, the patient is light and tachycardic, or a bolus has not yet reached the ventricle. The repeat TEE that decides surgery should be deliberate: conditions documented, each intervention confirmed to be in place, and the images reviewed with the surgeon. A study that shows persistent SAM with those conditions met is reliable. A study done during a hemodynamic swing in either direction is not. [REVIEW]

A second trap is to confuse the moderate MR of SAM with a primary repair failure and to plan a replacement for a valve that would be fine if the SAM were corrected. The surgeon needs to know which problem they are going back for.

**The surgical options and the mechanism each addresses.**

- **Sliding leaflet plasty (Carpentier).** Reduces the height of the posterior leaflet by detaching and re-attaching it lower on the annulus, which moves the coaptation point posteriorly. This is the classic correction for the excess-posterior-leaflet mechanism and is the first option for this patient, whose posterior leaflet was only partially reduced. [REVIEW]
- **Additional leaflet resection or folding plasty.** Removes or folds surplus posterior leaflet tissue for the same purpose with less dissection. [REVIEW]
- **Anterior leaflet shortening or resection.** Addresses excess anterior leaflet directly, less commonly done.
- **A larger ring, or replacing a complete ring with a band.** Enlarges the orifice, moves the coaptation point back, and reduces the tissue pushed toward the outflow tract. Carries a risk of recurrent MR if the annulus was the problem. [REVIEW]
- **Edge-to-edge (Alfieri) stitch.** Fixes the anterior leaflet to the posterior leaflet at the center, which tethers the anterior leaflet and prevents it from being drawn into the outflow tract. Fast and effective but creates a double orifice, raises the transmitral gradient, and is a compromise. Useful as a bailout. [REVIEW]
- **Septal myectomy.** For the patient whose obstruction is really from a thick basal septum. Can be done through the aortic valve or through the mitral orifice. Less relevant here where the septum is only mildly thick.
- **Valve replacement.** The last resort when the leaflet anatomy cannot be made to work. Replaces a living repair with a prosthesis in a 63-year-old, which is the outcome the whole operation was designed to avoid. [REVIEW]
- **Papillary muscle relocation or chordal interventions.** Reported for specific mechanisms. [REVIEW]

**Would I send her back now?** I would arrange the controlled TEE in the next one to two hours, with the surgeon present, having confirmed the inotrope is off, the rhythm is sinus, the esmolol is at the dose that produced the slowest tolerated rate, the phenylephrine is at the dose that produces the best pressure, and that no further volume helps. If the study shows what the twelve-hour study showed, she goes back for a sliding plasty with or without ring revision, with the Alfieri stitch as the bailout, and with a valve replacement only if the repair cannot be salvaged. The rising lactate and falling urine output mean this cannot wait until tomorrow. If, unusually, the controlled study shows the SAM has resolved, the plan is a slow wean of phenylephrine with the probe in, and a low threshold to return. [REVIEW]

**How long to persist.** There is no evidence-based answer. Series describe medical management over hours to a few days, with reoperation reserved for the hemodynamically compromised. The honest rule is that the duration of medical management should be set by the patient's organs, not by a number of hours: a patient who is perfusing on a modest vasoconstrictor can be given a day or more to settle. A patient who is accumulating lactate and fluid on a vasoconstrictor she cannot come off has already declared the answer. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: The controlled TEE confirms persistent SAM. In the operating room, before any revision, the surgeon asks you to help assess the repair again on bypass-ready conditions and after any correction. What loading conditions and measurements do you want for each study, and what is the risk of declaring the correction successful before the chest is closed?
questions.modelAnswer:
The 2020 ASE/SCA/STS guideline on intraoperative TEE for surgical decision-making is explicit that the post-repair assessment must be made under physiologic loading conditions, and that a study done on a ventricle that is empty, vasodilated, or on an inotrope will miss or exaggerate SAM. [REVIEW]

**For the pre-revision study.** The surgeon wants to know the mechanism before opening the atrium: the posterior leaflet height, the anterior leaflet length, the coaptation-to-septum distance, the position of the coaptation point relative to the annular plane, the septal thickness, the ring, and the direction and severity of the MR jet. The Varghese and Adams criteria give a framework for these measurements and should be the ones used so that the surgeon and the echocardiographer are speaking the same language. The exact values are to be looked up. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

**For the post-revision study.** The conditions must be physiological before the leaflet is judged: the heart filled to a normal end-diastolic dimension, the inotrope off (or at the minimum the surgeon will accept for separation), the afterload at a normal systemic pressure, and the rhythm sinus or AV paced at a normal rate. A ventricle just off bypass that is empty, hyperdynamic, on epinephrine, and vasodilated will show SAM that is not real, and a ventricle that has been overfilled and vasoconstricted for the study will hide SAM that is. The guideline recommends an afterload challenge (phenylephrine to a normal pressure) when there is doubt, and some surgeons will specifically ask for a brief provocation with reduced preload or a small inotrope dose to confirm the repair holds under the conditions it will meet in the ICU. Whether to provoke is a judgment call and belongs to the surgeon. [REVIEW]

The measurements for the post-revision study: residual SAM (chordal only, or leaflet with septal contact), the LVOT gradient by continuous-wave Doppler, the presence and direction of any MR jet, the transmitral gradient (particularly after an Alfieri stitch or a smaller ring), the coaptation-to-septum distance, and the coaptation length. [REVIEW]

**The risk of declaring success too early.** The ventricle the surgeon sees after a revision is not the ventricle the ICU will have at 03:00. Warming, vasodilation, diuresis, pain, tachycardia, and the loss of the atrial kick to postoperative atrial fibrillation will all shrink the cavity and raise the ejection velocity. A repair that is free of SAM on an overfilled, vasoconstricted, slow heart can obstruct eight hours later. The study that matters is the one on physiologic conditions with an afterload challenge, and the handoff to the ICU should state explicitly what conditions were tested and what the LVOT gradient was under them, so that the overnight team knows what the repair tolerates. The ICU plan should then protect those conditions: no inotrope, sinus or atrial pacing, volume kept up, phenylephrine for pressure, beta blockade continued, and a low threshold for the probe to go back in. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]

stages.title: The wider pattern
stages.narrative:
She underwent a sliding plasty and ring revision. The post-revision TEE under physiologic conditions and after an afterload challenge showed no SAM, a low LVOT gradient, and trivial MR. She returned to the CTICU on no inotrope, a low-dose vasoconstrictor that was weaned overnight, and a beta blocker, and was extubated the next morning. [REVIEW]

On morning rounds the attending asks you to generalize. Four patients are on the unit: a woman after aortic valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis with a thick basal septum who is hypotensive on an inotrope, a man two days after septal myectomy with a new gradient, a patient in septic shock with a small hyperdynamic LV who worsened when norepinephrine was switched to a mixed inotrope, and a patient with takotsubo cardiomyopathy and apical ballooning in cardiogenic shock. The attending asks: what from this case generalizes to each, and what does not?

questions.prompt: For each of the four patients, say whether dynamic LVOT obstruction is likely, by what mechanism, which parts of the SAM management plan carry over, and what is different.
questions.modelAnswer:
The common thread is that dynamic LVOT obstruction is a loading-condition disease. Wherever the LV is small, fast, and hypercontractile against a narrowed outflow tract, SAM and a dynamic gradient can appear, and wherever that is the mechanism of hypotension, inotropes and vasodilators will make it worse and volume, vasoconstriction, and slowing will make it better. The differences lie in the anatomy of the narrowing and in what else is going on.

**Post-AVR with septal hypertrophy.** Highly likely. A patient with long-standing aortic stenosis has a hypertrophied, small-cavity LV and often a thick basal septum. Removing the fixed obstruction at the valve unmasks the dynamic one below it: the ventricle that was ejecting against a stenotic valve now ejects against nothing, the velocity through the narrowed subvalvular region rises, and the anterior leaflet is pulled across. This is well described and is one reason some surgeons perform a myectomy at the time of AVR when the septum is thick. Everything from the SAM plan carries over: inotrope off, fill, vasoconstrict, slow, beta block, atrial pacing. What is different is that the obstruction is septal rather than mitral in origin, so the surgical correction, if medical management fails, is a myectomy rather than a leaflet procedure, and the mitral valve is usually intact so the MR is less of a feature. Also different: the patient may have a stiff hypertrophied ventricle with real diastolic dysfunction, so the volume strategy reaches congestion faster. [REVIEW]

**Post-myectomy.** Possible, and the question is whether the resection was adequate. The 2024 AHA/ACC HCM guideline frames residual obstruction after myectomy in terms of the provoked gradient, and an intraoperative TEE under physiological conditions is standard. Early postoperative obstruction can be from inadequate resection, from a mitral valve abnormality that was not addressed (anomalous papillary muscle insertion, excess leaflet length), or from the same loading-condition problem as any post-bypass ventricle. The management plan carries over fully. What is different is that the threshold for return to the operating room is higher for a loading problem in a patient whose anatomy was just addressed, and that a persistent gradient needs a conversation about mechanism (residual septum versus mitral apparatus) before a re-resection. Beta blockade in this population is both treatment and the medication they came in on. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

**Sepsis with a hyperdynamic LV.** Underappreciated and probably common. Septic patients are vasodilated, often hypovolemic, tachycardic, and catecholamine-driven, and a small proportion develop dynamic LVOT obstruction, with or without SAM, that is unmasked or worsened when a mixed inotrope (dobutamine, epinephrine) is added for a presumed low-output state. The patient who gets worse on dobutamine should be examined for this. The plan carries over: stop the inotrope, fill, use a pure vasoconstrictor, consider cautious beta blockade (which has its own small literature in sepsis, with esmolol and landiolol studied for rate control). What is different is that volume is less constrained by a stiff ventricle, the heart is usually structurally normal, the obstruction resolves as the sepsis resolves, and there is no surgical option. Also different: the diagnosis is easily missed because nobody is looking, which is an argument for echo in every septic patient who deteriorates on an inotrope. [REVIEW]

**Takotsubo with apical ballooning.** A known and dangerous combination. With the apex and mid-ventricle akinetic, the preserved basal segments become hypercontractile, the basal cavity narrows, and the anterior mitral leaflet is drawn into the outflow tract. A proportion of takotsubo patients in shock have LVOT obstruction rather than, or in addition to, pump failure, and the two require opposite treatments. The patient with obstruction gets worse on catecholamines and better on volume and a vasoconstrictor, and beta blockade is reasonable where the pressure permits. The patient with pump failure and no obstruction may need an inotrope or mechanical support. The echo distinguishes them and must be done before the inotrope is chosen. What carries over: the whole medical plan, when obstruction is present. What is different: the akinetic apex means that the ventricle has a low stroke volume regardless of the obstruction, so there is a ceiling on what afterload and volume can achieve, and mechanical support (an intra-aortic balloon pump worsens the obstruction, a transvalvular device has its own problems in a ventricle with an obstructed outflow tract and an akinetic apex) is a difficult conversation. [REVIEW]

**What generalizes.** The hemodynamic signature (worse with inotropes and vasodilators, better with volume and vasoconstrictors), the first moves (stop the inotrope, fill, vasoconstrict, slow, restore the atrial kick), the echo features (late-peaking dagger-shaped Doppler, septal contact, eccentric posterior MR), the contraindication to the intra-aortic balloon pump, and the trap of assessing the response under uncontrolled loading conditions. What does not generalize is the surgical pathway, which exists only where there is an anatomic substrate to correct. The question to ask on every hypotensive patient who gets worse when the inotrope goes up is the same: is the ventricle too empty and too fast, and is something in the way?

teachingPoints:
- Hypotension that worsens with inotropes and vasodilators and improves with volume and vasoconstrictors is dynamic LVOT obstruction until the echo says otherwise. The reflexive response to hypotension (more inotrope) is the one that harms.
- SAM after mitral repair results from anterior displacement of the coaptation point. Risk factors: excess posterior leaflet height, a small or complete ring, septal hypertrophy, a small hyperdynamic LV, anterior papillary displacement, redundant leaflets. The intensivist controls only the cavity size, the heart rate, and the afterload.
- The differential (bleeding, tamponade, vasoplegia, RV failure, residual MR, ring obstruction, circumflex injury) is managed by the same first moves except circumflex injury, which is why the ECG goes with the volume and the phenylephrine.
- Medical management: inotrope off, volume to a larger cavity, pure vasoconstrictor, beta blockade, slow sinus or atrial pacing, stop all vasodilators, no intra-aortic balloon pump. Each move either enlarges the cavity, slows ejection, or raises the pressure beyond the obstruction.
- The MR of SAM is a consequence of the obstruction and usually resolves with it. Do not plan a replacement for a repair that would work if the SAM were fixed.
- Medical management has failed when the gradient and MR persist under optimized conditions, the vasoconstrictor cannot be weaned, the organs are suffering, and further volume produces congestion without relief. Duration is set by the patient's organs, not by a clock.
- The TEE that decides surgery must be done under controlled, documented loading conditions. A study done during a hemodynamic swing in either direction is unreliable, and SAM called fixed on an overfilled vasoconstricted heart will return at 03:00.
- Surgical options address the mechanism: sliding plasty and resection for posterior leaflet height, a larger ring for annular reduction, the Alfieri stitch as a bailout, myectomy for the septum, replacement last.
- The same physiology appears after AVR with a thick septum, after myectomy, in sepsis on an inotrope, and in takotsubo. The medical plan generalizes. The surgical pathway does not.
pitfalls:
- Going up on epinephrine for hypotension with a new systolic murmur after mitral repair.
- Interpreting the eccentric MR of SAM as a failed repair and calling for a replacement.
- Treating pulmonary congestion from SAM-related MR with diuresis and vasodilators.
- Placing an intra-aortic balloon pump for hypotension in a patient with dynamic LVOT obstruction.
- Declaring SAM resolved on a TEE done while the patient is maximally optimized, then weaning the phenylephrine and extubating.
- Declaring medical management failed on a TEE done during a hemodynamic swing.
- Borrowing the HCM gradient threshold as if it defined when a postoperative patient needs reoperation.
- Forgetting circumflex injury as the one item on the differential that volume and phenylephrine do not treat.
- Missing the same physiology in the septic or takotsubo patient who deteriorated on dobutamine because nobody put a probe on the chest.
controversies:
**How long to persist medically before re-repair.** Series describe anything from hours to days of medical management, and reoperation rates for SAM in modern series are low. There is no trial and no agreed duration. One view holds that persistent SAM with a high gradient and significant MR at the end of the operation should be corrected before leaving the operating room, because the ICU will only make the loading conditions worse. Another holds that most SAM settles with time and that an early return commits the patient to a second bypass run for a problem that would have resolved. Both are defensible and the decision belongs to the surgeon with the echo in hand. [REVIEW]

**Prophylactic intraoperative measures.** Sliding plasty, limiting posterior leaflet height, choosing a larger ring or a band, and intraoperative TEE risk stratification (Varghese and Adams) are all used to prevent SAM. Whether a specific leaflet height threshold or ring size reliably predicts SAM, and whether the prophylactic measures carry a cost in repair durability, is debated. Surgeons at high-volume centers have strong and divergent views. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]

**Esmolol versus landiolol versus no beta blocker.** Beta blockade is physiologically sound and widely used, but it reduces contractility in a ventricle just off bypass and can drop the pressure in a patient who is already hypotensive. Some intensivists rely on volume and phenylephrine alone and add a beta blocker only if the heart rate stays high. Landiolol is more selective and shorter-acting than esmolol and is preferred in some units, mostly on pharmacological grounds, with limited comparative evidence in this setting. [REVIEW]

**The gradient threshold that matters.** The HCM guideline thresholds for defining obstruction are commonly borrowed for the postoperative patient, but the question in the ICU is not whether to do a myectomy. A modest gradient with hypotension and MR matters, and a higher gradient in a stable patient with no MR may not. The gradient should be interpreted with the pressure, the MR, and the loading conditions, not against a fixed cutoff. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

**Vasopressin versus phenylephrine.** Both are used. Vasopressin spares the beta receptor entirely and does not cause reflex bradycardia. Phenylephrine causes a helpful reflex bradycardia and is more familiar. There is no comparison in this setting. [NMH protocol, insert]
